letters.title: Galatians
letters.audiencePortrait: Congregations Paul planted in south Galatia — Gentile believers now being told they must take on the Mosaic law to belong.
letters.occasion: Rival teachers have followed him into churches he had only recently founded, demanding circumcision. He writes in heat because the gospel he already preached there is being rewritten: Christ plus Torah. This is not a general treatise. It is a rescue of his own plants.

outline.heading: No other gospel
outline.summary: Astonishment and anathema; the gospel is not his to revise.

outline.heading: Independent apostleship
outline.summary: Damascus, Jerusalem, and the clash with Peter at Antioch.

outline.heading: Promise, not law
outline.summary: Abraham, the curse of the law, sons rather than slaves.

outline.heading: Freedom’s fruit
outline.summary: Spirit against flesh; bear one another’s burdens.

outline.heading: Boast in the cross
outline.summary: Large letters, a new creation, no other boast.

letters.narrowedAudience: These are his own churches. The anger is pastoral, not distant: he can appeal to a gospel they already received from his mouth.

people.name: Peter (Cephas)
people.role: Named in the Antioch clash — another apostle in the same story.

people.name: Barnabas
people.role: Companion in the earlier mission; named with Peter at Antioch.

letters.datingNote: Consensus pins this just after the first journey, from Antioch, before the Jerusalem council. The wider Protestant debate is south Galatia (Acts 13–14 cities) versus north Galatia, which would move the letter later, into the third-journey years.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 13–14
actsAnchors.note: South-Galatian plants: Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 15:1–11
actsAnchors.note: Jerusalem council on Gentile circumcision — the same crisis Galatians names.

debated.originNote: Early south-Galatia from Antioch, or later from Ephesus / Macedonia if north Galatia.
debated.debateNote: South vs north Galatia is the main Protestant fork. The letter still names churches Paul had already preached in.

letters.title: 1 Thessalonians
letters.audiencePortrait: A young church Paul planted in a few weeks, then was forced to leave under hostility.
letters.occasion: Timothy has returned to Paul in Corinth with news: the Thessalonians are standing, but they grieve believers who died before the Lord’s coming. Paul writes to stabilize a church that had almost no time with him, and to say the dead in Christ are not left out.

outline.heading: Thanksgiving
outline.summary: Their faith became known in Macedonia and Achaia.

outline.heading: The visit remembered
outline.summary: Integrity of ministry; Timothy’s report and Paul’s longing.

outline.heading: Holiness and work
outline.summary: Please God; live quietly; a holy people in a watching city.

outline.heading: The coming
outline.summary: The dead in Christ; times and seasons; awake, not asleep.

outline.heading: Community life
outline.summary: Respect, prayer, the God of peace who will do it.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: Sent back to Thessalonica; his report occasions the letter.

people.name: Silas
people.role: Co-sender; companion on the second journey.

letters.datingNote: Among the tightest dates in the corpus. Acts 18 places Paul in Corinth when Gallio is proconsul; 1 Thessalonians is written from that stay after Timothy returns.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 17:1–10
actsAnchors.note: The plant in Thessalonica, then the night flight.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 18:1–5
actsAnchors.note: Paul in Corinth; Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 18:12–17
actsAnchors.note: Gallio in Achaia — the main external year-marker.

debated.debateNote: Protestants agree on Corinth and the second journey. The range only wiggles by a year around Gallio.

letters.title: 2 Thessalonians
letters.audiencePortrait: The same planted church, months later, unsettled by rumor.
letters.occasion: Word has spread that the Day of the Lord has already come. Some have quit ordinary work. Paul writes to correct the rumor, name what must precede the Day, and command quiet labor — a follow-up while he is still in Corinth.

outline.heading: Thanksgiving in persecution
outline.summary: God will repay; the church is counted worthy.

outline.heading: The Day has not come
outline.summary: Rebellion and the man of lawlessness first.

outline.heading: Idle disruption
outline.summary: Work, imitate Paul, warn the idle as a brother.

outline.heading: Benediction
outline.summary: Peace, and a signed greeting as a mark of genuineness.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: Co-sender, as in the first letter.

people.name: Silas
people.role: Co-sender.

letters.datingNote: Consensus: a short follow-up from Corinth after 1 Thessalonians. Wider Protestant discussion is how many months later, not whether Paul is still the writer in the narrative of the text.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 18:1–11
actsAnchors.note: The long Corinthian stay that can hold both Thessalonian letters.

debated.debateNote: Some Protestants read it as almost simultaneous with 1 Thessalonians; others a year later. Same city, same church.

letters.title: 1 Corinthians
letters.audiencePortrait: The church Paul planted in a status-conscious port — gifted, divided, and still entangled with the culture around it.
letters.occasion: Chloe’s people report factions, a case of incest, and lawsuits. A letter from Corinth has also arrived with questions about marriage, food, worship, and resurrection. Paul writes from Ephesus to pull a gifted church back under the word of the cross.

outline.heading: Divisions and the cross
outline.summary: Not wisdom, not leaders — the crucified Lord.

outline.heading: Holiness in the body
outline.summary: Discipline, courts, sexual ethics in a port city.

outline.heading: Answers to their letter
outline.summary: Marriage, food, and the temples of the city.

outline.heading: Worship
outline.summary: The table, gifts, and a still more excellent way.

outline.heading: Resurrection
outline.summary: If Christ is not raised, faith is empty.

outline.heading: Collection and travel
outline.summary: Jerusalem’s poor; Timothy; a hoped-for visit.

people.name: Chloe’s people
people.role: Bring the report of divisions.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: To be sent on to Corinth.

people.name: Apollos
people.role: A name around which factions have formed.

letters.datingNote: Written from Ephesus during the long third-journey stay. Acts 19 and 1 Corinthians 16:8 (“I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost”) lock the origin.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 18:1–11
actsAnchors.note: Paul plants Corinth and stays eighteen months.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 19:1–10
actsAnchors.note: The Ephesian stay from which he writes.

debated.debateNote: Origin is not in serious Protestant doubt. The year slides with how one counts the Ephesian stay.

letters.title: 2 Corinthians
letters.occasion: Titus has met Paul in Macedonia with mixed but hopeful news: the severe letter worked, yet rivals still undermine his apostleship. Paul defends a ministry of weakness, reopens the Jerusalem collection, and warns he will come a third time.
letters.audiencePortrait: The same Corinthian church, after a painful visit and a severe letter that nearly broke the relationship.

outline.heading: Comfort in affliction
outline.summary: Why he did not come; the tearful letter.

outline.heading: New-covenant ministry
outline.summary: Jars of clay; reconciliation; Titus’s report.

outline.heading: The collection
outline.summary: Grace, not pressure, for the saints in Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Defense against rivals
outline.summary: Boasting in weakness; the thorn; a coming visit.

people.name: Titus
people.role: Bearer of news and of the collection appeal.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: Co-sender.

letters.datingNote: From Macedonia after leaving Ephesus, on the way back toward Corinth. Acts 20:1–3 is the road; 2 Corinthians 2 and 7 are the feelings.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 20:1–3
actsAnchors.note: Macedonia, then three months in Greece.

debated.debateNote: Whether chapters 10–13 are a later add-on is discussed; the from-Macedonia setting is not.

letters.title: Romans
letters.audiencePortrait: A mixed Jewish–Gentile church in the imperial capital that Paul did not plant and has never visited.
letters.occasion: Paul is about to take the collection to Jerusalem, then hopes to visit Rome on the way to Spain. He writes a full statement of the gospel to a church he did not found — to unify Jew and Gentile under one mercy, and to ask their help for a western mission. Phoebe of Cenchreae carries the letter.

outline.heading: The gospel of God
outline.summary: Power for salvation, Jew first and also Greek.

outline.heading: Universal need
outline.summary: Gentiles, Jews, the whole world accountable.

outline.heading: Justified by faith
outline.summary: Abraham, peace with God, Adam and Christ.

outline.heading: Union and the Spirit
outline.summary: Dead to sin; no condemnation; creation groaning.

outline.heading: Israel and mercy
outline.summary: God’s faithfulness to Israel is not revoked.

outline.heading: A living sacrifice
outline.summary: One body; the weak and the strong; welcome.

outline.heading: Spain, Phoebe, names
outline.summary: Travel plans and a long list of people he has not yet hugged.

letters.narrowedAudience: Rome is not Corinth. He cannot lean on shared memory of a founding visit. The argument has to carry strangers in the capital — a church already walking a Jew–Gentile tightrope under imperial eyes. That is why origin and destination matter: a reasoned gospel for an unvisited mixed church, written from a plant that knew him too well.

people.name: Phoebe
people.role: Servant of the church at Cenchreae; likely bearer of the letter.

people.name: Priscilla & Aquila
people.role: Greeted in Rome; earlier coworkers in Corinth and Ephesus.

people.name: Gaius
people.role: Host in Corinth, named as Paul writes.

letters.datingNote: From Corinth at the close of the third journey. Gaius and Erastus in Romans 16 match Acts 20:2–3. Peter later names Paul’s letters as Scripture — including this kind of “hard to understand” writing.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 20:2–3
actsAnchors.note: Three months in Greece — the Corinthian window for Romans.

otherWitness.label: 2 Peter 3:15–16
otherWitness.note: Peter on “our beloved brother Paul” and his letters.

debated.debateNote: From-Corinth is the Protestant consensus. The year moves with how one counts the third journey’s end.

letters.title: Philemon
letters.audiencePortrait: Philemon, a house-church host in Colossae, and the household gathered in his home — including, by implication, the enslaved Onesimus.
letters.occasion: Onesimus has come to Paul in custody, become a believer, and is being sent back. Paul asks Philemon to receive him as a brother, hints at manumission, and offers to pay any debt. The whole letter is persuasion aimed at one man, read aloud in a living room.

outline.heading: Greeting and thanks
outline.summary: Partnership, love, and refreshment of the saints.

outline.heading: The appeal
outline.summary: Not a command: a son, a brother, more than a slave.

outline.heading: Charge it to me
outline.summary: Welcome him as you would me; prepare a guest room.

outline.heading: The circle
outline.summary: The same coworkers named in Colossians.

letters.narrowedAudience: Ephesians can speak of the cosmic church in general terms. Philemon cannot. The audience is one host, one runaway, one house. Brotherhood has to mean a changed seat at a particular table, or the letter has failed. That is why it is not a miniature Ephesians: same prison, same courier circle, utterly different scale.

people.name: Philemon
people.role: Host of the Colossian house church; the one who must decide.

people.name: Onesimus
people.role: The runaway, now a believer, sent back with the letter.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: Co-sender.

letters.datingNote: Paired with Colossians by Onesimus and Tychicus. Consensus: Rome, house arrest (Acts 28). Wider Protestant debate: Ephesus in the mid-50s (shorter walk for a runaway) or, less often, Caesarea.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 28:16, 30–31
actsAnchors.note: House arrest in Rome — the consensus prison.

letterAnchors.label: Colossians 4:7–9
letterAnchors.note: Onesimus and Tychicus on the same road.

debated.originNote: Rome (Acts 28) is the consensus; Ephesus in the 50s is the main Protestant alternative.
debated.debateNote: Prison location — Rome, Ephesus, or (less often) Caesarea — is the fork, not whether Paul wrote it.

letters.title: Colossians
letters.audiencePortrait: A church Paul did not found — planted by Epaphras in the Lycus valley — now flirting with a syncretistic “philosophy.”
letters.occasion: Epaphras has reached Paul with news of a teaching that mixes Jewish observances, visionary religion, and elemental powers. Paul writes to exalt Christ over every power and to insist that fullness is already in him, not in extra rites. He has not seen their faces.

outline.heading: Christ the image
outline.summary: The hymn; all things held together; you who were alienated.

outline.heading: Paul’s labor
outline.summary: A struggle for those who have not seen his face.

outline.heading: Against the philosophy
outline.summary: Fullness in Christ; shadows, not substance.

outline.heading: Risen life
outline.summary: Put on the new self; households; prayer and speech.

outline.heading: Tychicus and Onesimus
outline.summary: The same courier team as Philemon.

letters.narrowedAudience: He is writing to a church he did not plant. Authority here rests on the gospel they received from Epaphras, and on Christ’s supremacy, not on a shared founding story.

people.name: Epaphras
people.role: Founder of the Colossian church; now with Paul.

people.name: Tychicus
people.role: Bearer of the letter.

people.name: Onesimus
people.role: Travels with Tychicus; also the subject of Philemon.

letters.datingNote: Companion to Philemon. Consensus: Rome, AD 60–62. Wider Protestant debate is the same prison-location fork (Rome / Ephesus / Caesarea), not a different century.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 19:10
actsAnchors.note: All Asia hears the word from Ephesus — the road Epaphras likely walked.

debated.debateNote: Same prison debate as Philemon. The letter still presents Paul in chains writing to a church he has not visited.

letters.title: Ephesians
letters.audiencePortrait: Churches in Asia — Ephesus and likely a circular run of congregations — not a single crisis-bound plant.
letters.occasion: There is little local fire to put out. The letter offers a measured account of identity in Christ, the unity of Jew and Gentile in one new humanity, and a life that walks worthy of that calling. It reads more like a liturgical briefing than a reply to questions.

outline.heading: Blessing in Christ
outline.summary: Every spiritual blessing; a prayer for sight.

outline.heading: One new humanity
outline.summary: Grace; the mystery; Paul on his knees for them.

outline.heading: Unity and gifts
outline.summary: One body, many gifts, toward maturity.

outline.heading: Walk
outline.summary: New self, light, and households under the same Lord.

outline.heading: Armor
outline.summary: Stand; Tychicus will tell you how I am.

letters.narrowedAudience: The audience is regional and relatively calm. That is why it sounds different from Corinth’s emergency mail — and why, beside Philemon, the same imprisonment can produce both cosmic ecclesiology and a household appeal.

people.name: Tychicus
people.role: Bearer, as in Colossians.

letters.datingNote: Consensus: Rome, with Colossians, possibly circular (some early copies lack “in Ephesus”). Wider Protestant debate: the same prison location, and whether it is a local letter or a round-robin to Asia.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 20:17–31
actsAnchors.note: Farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus.

debated.debateNote: Circular vs local, and which prison, are the Protestant questions. The letter still speaks from chains.

letters.title: Philippians
letters.audiencePortrait: The church Paul planted in Philippi — his first European congregation, and the one that kept sending help.
letters.occasion: They have sent a gift through Epaphroditus, who fell ill. Paul writes from custody to thank them, to interpret his chains as gospel advance, to urge unity in the mind of Christ, and to warn against rivals. Joy here is not mood. It is defiance with reasons.

outline.heading: Partnership in the gospel
outline.summary: Chains that preach; to live is Christ.

outline.heading: The mind of Christ
outline.summary: The hymn; Timothy and Epaphroditus on the road.

outline.heading: Knowing Christ
outline.summary: Rubbish, resurrection, citizens of heaven.

outline.heading: Peace and the gift
outline.summary: Euodia and Syntyche; contentment; the offering received.

people.name: Epaphroditus
people.role: Their messenger; ill, now sent home with honor.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: To be sent to Philippi soon.

people.name: Euodia & Syntyche
people.role: Coworkers asked to agree in the Lord.

letters.datingNote: Consensus: Rome. A strong Protestant minority prefers Ephesus in the mid-50s, because Epaphroditus’s round trip is easier from Asia than from Italy.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 16:11–40
actsAnchors.note: The plant: the river, Lydia, the jailer.

debated.originNote: Rome is the consensus; Ephesus shortens Epaphroditus’s travel.
debated.debateNote: The “praetorium” in 1:13 can fit Rome or a provincial capital. That is the fork.

letters.title: 1 Timothy
letters.audiencePortrait: Timothy, Paul’s delegate left in Ephesus — not the Ephesian church as a whole.
letters.occasion: Paul has left Timothy to stop certain teachers and to appoint qualified overseers and deacons. The letter is a charge to a coworker: how to order a household of God already under pressure from speculative teaching and a leadership vacuum.

outline.heading: The charge
outline.summary: No other doctrine; mercy to the worst of sinners.

outline.heading: Prayer and household order
outline.summary: Public prayer; overseers and deacons.

outline.heading: The good minister
outline.summary: Train for godliness; watch your life and teaching.

outline.heading: Widows, elders, slaves
outline.summary: Honor with discernment; do not be hasty in laying on hands.

outline.heading: Godliness and money
outline.summary: Fight the fight; the good confession; true wealth.

letters.narrowedAudience: This is not Romans. It is not even a church letter. The “you” is singular: a younger coworker told how to appoint, refuse, and guard. Church order here is a field manual, not a constitution mailed to a congregation. Read it as a charge, or the tone will feel oddly managerial.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: The addressee; left in Ephesus to stop false teachers and appoint leaders.

people.name: Hymenaeus & Alexander
people.role: Named as having shipwrecked faith.

letters.datingNote: Consensus: after Acts, from Macedonia, Timothy stationed in Ephesus. Wider Protestant debate: whether Paul is released after Acts 28 and travels again, or whether 1 Timothy fits an earlier leave-taking during the third journey.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 19:21–22
actsAnchors.note: Timothy already serving the Ephesian work.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 20:17–31
actsAnchors.note: The charge to Ephesian elders — same city, same concerns.

debated.debateNote: After-Acts travel vs an earlier leave-taking. The letter still addresses Timothy in Ephesus, not the church as a whole.

letters.title: Titus
letters.audiencePortrait: Titus, left on Crete to appoint elders in every town — a delegate on an unfinished island.
letters.occasion: Crete has scattered groups of believers and a reputation Paul does not flatter. Titus must appoint elders, silence rebellious teachers, and teach a grace that trains a people for good works. The letter is short because the task is concrete.

outline.heading: Elders and opposition
outline.summary: Qualifications for every town; Cretan teachers silenced.

outline.heading: Grace that trains
outline.summary: Households; the appearing of grace, not mere rule.

outline.heading: Ready for good works
outline.summary: Regeneration, not quarrels; send Zenas and Apollos; winter at Nicopolis.

letters.narrowedAudience: Like 1 Timothy, the audience is one man with a job. Crete is not receiving a theological treatise; Titus is receiving a to-do list baptized in grace. The doctrine of 2:11–14 exists to produce a people, and a people needs elders in every town.

people.name: Titus
people.role: The addressee; left on Crete to appoint elders.

people.name: Artemas / Tychicus
people.role: One of them will relieve Titus.

letters.datingNote: Consensus: same after-Acts window as 1 Timothy, on a trajectory toward Nicopolis (Titus 3:12). Crete is named in the letter; Acts records a Cretan stop on the voyage to Rome, which some Protestants connect.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 27:7–13
actsAnchors.note: The voyage hugs Crete — Fair Havens — before the storm.

consensus.originNote: Written on a trajectory toward wintering at Nicopolis.

debated.debateNote: When the Cretan work fits — after a release from Rome, or an earlier unrecorded visit — is the Protestant question.

letters.title: 2 Timothy
letters.audiencePortrait: Timothy, again — now receiving what reads as a last dispatch from a man who expects death.
letters.occasion: Paul is in a harsher Roman imprisonment. Some have deserted; Onesiphorus has not. He wants Timothy to come before winter, to bring Mark, a cloak, and the parchments, and to guard the deposit without shame. This is not church-planting mail. It is a dying charge.

outline.heading: Fan the gift
outline.summary: Not shame; the pattern of sound words; Onesiphorus unashamed of chains.

outline.heading: Soldier, athlete, farmer
outline.summary: Entrust to faithful people; the Lord knows those who are his.

outline.heading: Last days and Scripture
outline.summary: Godlessness; continue; all Scripture God-breathed.

outline.heading: Come before winter
outline.summary: Preach; the time of departure; names of the faithful and the deserters.

letters.narrowedAudience: 1 Thessalonians was written to a young church looking forward together. 2 Timothy is written to one protégé from a cell. The future tense of hope is still there, but the present tense is farewell: names, a cloak, a last visit. That is why it feels different in the hand.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: The addressee; told to come before winter.

people.name: Lois & Eunice
people.role: His grandmother and mother; sincere faith.

people.name: Onesiphorus
people.role: Not ashamed of the chain; sought Paul in Rome.

people.name: Luke
people.role: Alone with Paul.

letters.datingNote: Consensus: a final Roman imprisonment after Acts, AD 64–67. Wider Protestant debate is how to relate this harsher custody to the house arrest of Acts 28 — a release and a second arrest is the usual reconstruction. Peter, facing his own departure, also writes of Paul’s letters.

actsAnchors.label: Acts 28:16, 30–31
actsAnchors.note: The earlier, more open custody — different in tone from 2 Timothy.

otherWitness.label: 2 Peter 1:13–15
otherWitness.note: Peter also writes as a man near departure.

otherWitness.label: 2 Peter 3:15–16
otherWitness.note: Peter on Paul’s letters as Scripture.

debated.debateNote: How this custody relates to Acts 28 is the Protestant question. The letter still reads as a last charge from Rome to Timothy.
